insights.title: The shelf is one formula repeated 1,300 times
insights.finding: Caffeine (78%), B6 (72%), niacin (71%), B12 (71%), potassium (59%), sucralose (58%) and taurine (50%) form a commodity core present in most SKUs.
insights.why: Differentiation on the current axis is nearly impossible — you would be launching the same liquid with a different label.
insights.metric: 7 ingredients appear in half or more of all energy-drink SKUs

insights.title: Functional ingredients consumers ask for are almost absent
insights.finding: Ashwagandha 1.0% of SKUs, rhodiola 0.3%, lion's mane 0.1%, reishi 0.2%. Cordyceps, probiotics and any product literally naming itself nootropic or adaptogenic: zero.
insights.why: This is the clearest supply gap in the dataset — and it sits directly against the top-ranked consumer concept.
insights.metric: 0% of shelf names an adaptogen or nootropic

insights.title: Sweetener choice is synthetic by default
insights.finding: Sucralose 58% and acesulfame-K 42% dominate. Stevia is 12%, monk fruit 3.0%, allulose 0.5%.
insights.why: A natural-sweetener product is genuinely rare on shelf, not merely under-marketed.
insights.metric: Natural sweeteners are on under 1 in 8 SKUs

insights.title: Consumers rank 'natural' above 'sugar-free'
insights.finding: Top concepts: additional functional benefits 40.7%, natural sweeteners 39.4%, natural caffeine 38.4%, adaptogens 33.9%.
insights.why: The industry is optimising for sugar-free, which consumers did not rank first.
insights.metric: 39.4% would try a naturally-sweetened energy drink

insights.title: Gen X wants 'natural' more than Gen Z does
insights.finding: Functional benefits index 51.5% among Gen X vs 33.8% Gen Z; natural sweeteners 49.5% vs 36.5%.
insights.why: The natural positioning skews older than the category's marketing assumes. Boomers are not published for this question.
insights.metric: Gen X leads on 6 of the top 7 concepts

insights.title: Function and taste are joint first, not a trade-off
insights.finding: Top-2-box motivations: boost energy 77.8%, enjoy the taste 77.2%, stay awake 75.0%, improve focus 74.4%.
insights.why: A functional product that tastes mediocre loses half the motivation set. Both have to be true.
insights.metric: Taste ties with energy as the #1 reason to drink

insights.title: Sugar-free is table stakes, not white space
insights.finding: 72.3% of 2024–26 launches claim sugar-free, up from 48.5% in 2018–20. Cognitive/brain claims went 25.8% to 53.8%.
insights.why: Launching 'sugar-free' as the differentiator now means matching three quarters of the pipeline.
insights.metric: +23.8pp sugar-free, +28.0pp cognitive claims

insights.title: Beauty-function appeared from nothing
insights.finding: Hair/nails and skin claims went 0% of launches in 2018–20 to 10.6% in 2024–26.
insights.why: A new segment forming in real time — and precisely Alani Nu's positioning.
insights.metric: 0% → 10.6% in six years

insights.title: Only 6% of new brands ever reach $1M
insights.finding: 150 brands entered since 2019. Nine reached $1M trailing-12-month revenue. None reached $10M.
insights.why: This is the base rate to plan against. The realistic ceiling for a c-store entrant is single-digit millions.
insights.metric: 6% reach $1M · 0% reach $10M

insights.title: You cannot enter with a single SKU
insights.finding: Median revenue per SKU: $4K for one-SKU brands, $50K at 4–8 SKUs, $1.87M at 25+.
insights.why: Buyers allocate shelf to blocks, not orphans. Read a broad range as a necessary condition for scale.
insights.metric: 400x spread between 1-SKU and 25+-SKU brands

insights.title: 'Original' flavour is bleeding share to fruit
insights.finding: Original fell from 36.2% of category revenue in 2019 to 30.1% in 2025. Watermelon rose +4.8pp, Juneberry +4.6pp.
insights.why: The category is fragmenting toward specific and proprietary fruit flavours. Fruit Punch (-3.8pp) and Blue Razz (-1.5pp) show the losers are the generic ones.
insights.metric: Original -6.2pp in six years

insights.title: A third of revenue sits in one price band
insights.finding: $0.25–0.30 per ounce holds 33.9% of single-serve revenue on 177 SKUs — $7.4M revenue per SKU, double any other band.
insights.why: That is where consumers have shown willingness to pay. Above $0.40/oz is a graveyard: 45 SKUs, 0.4% of revenue.
insights.metric: $7.4M revenue per SKU at $0.25–0.30/oz

insights.title: Regional strongholds are real
insights.finding: Guayaki indexes 1,035 in California, 852 in Oregon, 692 in Colorado. Rip It indexes 512 in Michigan.
insights.why: Regional launches demonstrably work here — a concentrated beachhead is cheaper than national distribution.
insights.metric: 10x national share in a single state

insights.title: No legacy brand reaches the genuinely health-conscious
insights.finding: 'I consider my diet very healthy' — best brand indexes 91. 'Nutritional value is most important' — 92. Yet the category indexes 181 on 'influenced by the latest health food trends'.
insights.why: The category attracts trend-followers, not the health-driven. But Celsius and Alani Nu are absent from this panel, so read it as why they are winning rather than as open territory.
insights.metric: Every health attitude sits below index 100

insights.title: Two brands own two thirds of the market
insights.finding: Monster 38.2% and Red Bull 34.5% of US retail value in 2025; Celsius 10.6%.
insights.why: A challenger competes for the remaining third, and mostly against other challengers.
insights.metric: Top 2 = 72.7% of retail value

insights.title: Alani Nu is the breakout, and social data missed it
insights.finding: Alani Nu +84% in MULO and +96% in POS. Bang, which the site's mention-share panel ranked a top riser, actually fell 15.6%.
insights.why: Attention and demand diverge. Sales data should override social signals wherever they disagree.
insights.metric: +96% POS growth vs a -15.6% brand ranked as 'rising'

insights.title: The convergent thesis: natural + functional, priced at $0.25–0.30/oz
insights.finding: Four independent sources agree. Consumers rank natural and functional first (Mintel). The shelf is 58% sucralose with near-zero adaptogens (USDA). Health-oriented consumers are unreached by legacy brands (Simmons). The fastest-growing brands already occupy that space (POS + MULO).
insights.why: This is the only claim in the analysis supported by stated preference, formulation, consumer profiling and actual sales at the same time.
insights.metric: 4 sources · 1 conclusion

insights.title: Strawberry is the most over-launched flavour
insights.finding: 9.6% of recent launches are strawberry; it is 0.1% of sales. Lime, berry, cherry and orange follow the same pattern.
insights.why: Launch activity is a poor guide to demand. Watermelon is the exception — heavily launched and genuinely growing.
insights.metric: 9.6% of launches, 0.1% of sales

insights.title: A 210-row table overturned the headline
insights.finding: Euromonitor Passport measures every channel and puts the women's fitness audience at 12.1% of US retail value. An earlier estimate that used Mintel MULO to stand in for all non-convenience sales put it at 18.4% — MULO covers top brands only, so it over-weights Celsius and Alani Nu.
insights.why: Row count and analytical value are unrelated. PDI has 1.09 billion rows and sees one channel; Passport has 210 and sees all of them. Triangulate before trusting any single source.
insights.metric: women 18.4% → 12.1% after re-anchoring

insights.title: Nobody is building for the alcohol occasion
insights.finding: 16% of consumers use energy drinks as an alcohol mixer and 14% as an alcohol alternative. A further 20% use them to replace coffee, against a coffee-crossover segment measuring 0.2% of convenience sales.
insights.why: These occasions are larger than most of the audiences the category segments on, and no major brand is positioned for them. Stated occasions run well ahead of what the shelf offers.
insights.metric: 30% combined alcohol-adjacent use, no dedicated products

insights.title: Energy shots are the one shrinking segment
insights.finding: Shots fell from $1.09B in 2019 to $0.87B in 2025, forecast to $0.75B by 2030. Drinks grew 13.9% in 2025 alone.
insights.why: The 2oz format is in structural decline in measured retail, whatever the trade press says about discretion and portability.
insights.metric: shots -20% since 2019 while drinks nearly doubled

insights.title: The $26.9B survives an independent check
insights.finding: Mintel publishes spend per household separately from its market total. Dividing one by the other implies 128-135M US households across seven years, against a Census count near 131-132M.
insights.why: Two separately derived figures agreeing to within a couple of percent is a real validation of the market size, not a restatement of it.
insights.metric: implied households within ~2% of Census, 2019-2025

now.label: US demand today (2025)
now.sub: Anchored on Euromonitor Passport all-channel brand shares, with the sub-threshold "others" allocated on PDI proportions and zero-sugar lines carved back out using the split PDI measures.

future.label: Projected US demand (2030)
future.sub: Mintel's central $38.6B forecast, split by extrapolating Passport's own 2021-2025 share drift and damping it for saturation.

why.Young adults: Still the biggest audience by far, and still growing in dollars — but its share erodes about 2-3 points a year in both channels as the category widens beyond it. Red Bull and Monster are each growing 15% in multi-outlet; they are not shrinking, they are being diluted.
why.Women (fitness & wellness): The clearest trend in the data. Went from 0.2% to 11.8% of convenience sales in six years, and is already 24% of multi-outlet sales where Celsius and Alani Nu concentrate. Alani Nu alone grew 84% year on year. Mintel's survey backs it: 39% of consumers want naturally-sweetened energy.
why.Gym & fitness: Flat in convenience for four years, and losing multi-outlet share as Bang (-8%) and Reign (-22%) decline. The RTD pre-workout idea is mature; the growth has migrated to the wellness framing rather than the performance one.
why.Shift workers & military: Slow structural decline. Value brands lose share whenever the category premiumises, and c-store traffic is the channel most exposed to that.
why.Calorie-cutters: The sharpest faller, and it is a definitional shift rather than a real collapse: sugar-free stopped being a distinct proposition. 72% of 2024-26 launches claim it, so it is now table stakes folded into every other audience.
why.Health-conscious adults: Small but compounding. Yerba mate and plant-caffeine brands sell mainly through natural grocery, which convenience data barely sees, so the true base is larger than 0.5%.
why.Gamers & creators: Understated everywhere in this data — G FUEL and Prime sell primarily through e-commerce and mass, and the 'other' channel that carries them grew 28% in 2025. Held at a floor of 1.6% for 2030 rather than trended, because both measured channels are blind to it.
why.Coffee drinkers: Early but real. Coffee-energy hybrids convert adults who reject the energy-drink identity, and the entry point is cold brew rather than the energy aisle.
why.Older functional users: Shots remain a niche in this dataset, though trade reporting suggests 2oz formats are outgrowing large cans in channels PDI does not cover.

channel.name: Women (fitness & wellness)
channel.why: The biggest single correction on the page. Celsius and Alani Nu sell overwhelmingly through grocery, mass and club — not the c-store cooler. They are 11.8% of convenience sales but 28.2% of multi-outlet, so counting only convenience halves this audience.

channel.name: Young adults
channel.why: Barely moves. Red Bull and Monster are the two brands with genuinely universal distribution, so their audience looks almost the same in every channel — 67.6% in convenience, 61.0% in multi-outlet.

channel.name: Gym & fitness
channel.why: Falls once other channels are counted. Performance brands are c-store-heavy impulse buys; in multi-outlet they are only 6.2%, and the two that do have grocery distribution are shrinking (Bang -8%, Reign -22%).

channel.name: Calorie-cutters
channel.why: Lower, because this group is defined by the zero-sugar lines of mainstream c-store brands rather than by any brand with broad grocery distribution.

channel.name: Shift workers & military
channel.why: Slightly lower. Value brands are a convenience-channel phenomenon almost by definition — nobody drives to a supermarket for a $1 can.

channel.name: Health-conscious adults
channel.why: Understated in both columns. Yerba mate and organic brands concentrate in natural grocery, a channel neither PDI nor MULO covers well.

channel.name: Gamers & creators
channel.why: Understated in both columns, badly. G FUEL and Prime sell mainly through e-commerce, which is inside Mintel's 'other' channel but invisible at brand level.

channel.name: Coffee drinkers
channel.why: Marginal either way at this size; coffee-energy hybrids are still a rounding error in measured retail.

channel.name: Older functional users
channel.why: Shots are a small slice of both channels in this data.

convenience.label: Convenience stores
convenience.note: Impulse and single-serve. The channel PDI measures — and the slowest-growing of the three.

other.label: All other
other.note: E-commerce, club, drug, foodservice. Fastest growing by a wide margin, and invisible in both PDI and MULO.

supermarket.label: Supermarkets
supermarket.note: Grocery. Where Celsius and Alani Nu concentrate, which is why the c-store view understates women.

now.label: US demand today (2025)
now.sub: All channels. Convenience shares measured from PDI, multi-outlet from Mintel MULO brand sales, blended on Mintel channel weights.

future.label: Projected US demand (2030)
future.sub: Mintel's central forecast of $38.6B, split by extrapolating each audience's measured share drift and damping it for saturation.

alt_mulo.label: Earlier estimate — convenience blended with Mintel MULO
alt_mulo.why_superseded: MULO covers top brands only, so using it to represent the whole non-convenience 40% over-weighted Celsius and Alani Nu. Euromonitor Passport measures every channel including e-commerce and covers the full brand list, so it replaces it.

segments_dw.label: Drinks vs shots
segments_dw.note: Energy shots are the one part of the category in outright decline: $1.09B in 2019 to $0.87B in 2025, and Mintel forecasts $0.75B by 2030. Drinks grew 13.9% in 2025 alone. Shots are 3.2% of the market and shrinking.

brand_dollars.note: Euromonitor Passport all-channel share applied to Mintel market value.

household.note: Mintel reports spend per household independently of its market total. Dividing one by the other implies 128-135M US households across seven years, against a Census count of roughly 131-132M. Two figures that were derived separately agree, which is a real check on the $26.9B rather than a restatement of it.

validation.freq_note: 40% of energy-drink consumers drink them several times a week or more — close to carbonated soft drinks at 47%, and ahead of sports drinks. This is a habit category, not an occasional treat.
validation.occ_note: The two rows at the bottom are the ones nobody is building for. 16% use energy drinks as an alcohol mixer and 14% as an alcohol alternative — together larger than most of the audiences on this page, and not captured by any of them. 20% use them to replace coffee, against a Coffee-crossover segment that measures 0.2% of convenience sales. Stated occasions are running well ahead of what the shelf offers.

women_pace.note: Annual gain in all-channel share, not the level. The level still rises every year, which is what makes the deceleration easy to miss: the segment added 4.1 points in 2023 and 1.0 in 2025. The site's own 2030 projection implies 1.84 points a year — 1.8x the most recent measured year — so the forecast is already leaning against the trend's own direction.

board.name: The Creator
board.role: Founded a challenger energy brand, exited to a strategic
says: Look at where the money per SKU is, not where the money is. Young adults × Original is $137M — and every dollar of it belongs to Red Bull. That is not an opportunity, that is a wall.
The cells I would kill for are Women × Punch and Women × Sour: growing 279% and 114%, and each SKU there earns eight to ten times the category median. Few competitors, proven money.
One SKU is not a launch. The data says one-SKU brands median $4K a year and 25+ SKU brands median $1.87M. Whatever we pick, we need a four-to-eight SKU platform on day one.

board.name: The Investor
board.role: CPG growth fund, led rounds in two beverage brands
says: I only care about one number on this site: women take 51% of all new demand through 2030. Roughly $6B. Everything else is a rounding error by comparison.

But I want to underwrite the risk honestly. That women's line rests on a six-year trend that has not slowed once. If Celsius and Alani are near saturation, we are underwriting 22% not 28%, and the whole thesis softens.
Six percent of new brands ever reach $1M in this data, and none reached $10M. Price the base rate in. We are not buying a lottery ticket, we are buying distribution.

board.name: The Retail Buyer
says: Your data is my channel, so let me correct the frame: I am 60% of this category and I am the *slow* 60%. Grocery and club grew faster last year.
I do not have shelf for another 16oz berry can. I have 86 of them from young-adult brands alone. Bring me something my planogram does not already have.
Watch the price band. A third of single-serve revenue sits at $0.25-0.30 per ounce, and that band earns $7.4M per SKU — double any other. Price outside it and I cannot justify the facing.

board.name: The Formulator
says: Seven ingredients appear in half of all SKUs. Caffeine, B6, niacin, B12, potassium, sucralose, taurine. The shelf is one formula repeated 1,300 times.
Sugar-free is not a differentiator any more — 72% of recent launches claim it. Natural sweetener is different: 39% of consumers say they want it and almost nobody ships it.
Careful with the survey. Stated interest in adaptogens is 34%; measured beauty-function launches went 0% to 10.6% and we still cannot see whether they sell. Intent is not sell-through.

views.text: Flavor. Women's brands are winning on fruit and novelty and there is visible headroom in punch, sour and grape.
Formulation. Flavor is a six-month lead at best; a natural-sweetener, natural-caffeine platform is defensible for years.
Neither, on my shelf. The unmet need is a *reason to displace* an existing facing. Novelty alone does not do it.

debate.resolve: They are answering different questions. Flavor gets you trial, formulation gets you retention, the buyer gates whether either happens. The data supports doing all three at once: a natural-sweetener platform, launched in the growing flavor cells, priced into the band the buyer can justify.

debate.q: Is the women's segment already taken?

views.text: Effectively, yes. Celsius and Alani Nu are 24% of multi-outlet between them and are owned by the same company now.
Taken at the top, wide open underneath. Three brands serve 211 SKUs against an audience adding $6B. Category consolidation creates shelf orphans.
One owner controlling both leaders is exactly when I go looking for a third option, for leverage if nothing else.

debate.resolve: Consolidation cuts both ways and the buyer's incentive is the tiebreaker. A credible third brand has a structural opening that did not exist before the acquisition.

debate.q: What about the gaps the tool surfaces?

views.text: Half of them are graveyards. Calorie-cutters x Tropical has 52 SKUs and $0.39M. That is not untried, that is tried and rejected.
Agreed, and that distinction is the most useful thing on this page. Zero SKUs is opportunity. Fifty SKUs and no revenue is a warning.
Which is why I want the untried list short and the failed list visible next to it. Otherwise the tool manufactures false confidence.

debate.resolve: The White Space Finder separates the two explicitly: fewer than 3 SKUs is untried, 8 or more with under $0.5M is a graveyard. Never read one as the other.

verdict.headline: A naturally-sweetened platform for the women's wellness audience, launched as a 4-8 SKU flavor family in the growing fruit and novelty cells, priced at $2.50–$2.99 per 16 oz can.
why: Takes 51% of all category growth to 2030 (+$6.0B), growing 17.2% a year against the category's 7.5%.
39.4% of consumers say they want natural sweeteners and almost nothing on shelf delivers it. Sugar-free alone is table stakes at 72% of launches.
Punch, sour-candy, berry and tropical for this audience all grow 12-279% a year and each SKU there earns 8-17x the category median revenue.

$2.50–$2.99 for the 16 oz can — about $0.16–$0.18 an ounce. That band returns $3.09M per SKU against $2.02M one rung up, and 43% of all 16 oz money sits in it. Do not price off the category's per-ounce figure: $0.25–$0.30/oz is a 12 oz number (79.5% of that band is 12 oz cans) and on a 16 oz can it means $4.00–$4.80, where 7 SKUs have ever earned $0.02M each.
One-SKU brands median $4K a year; 4-8 SKUs median $50K; 25+ median $1.87M. Launch as a platform, not a hero.
risks: 6% of new brands since 2019 reached $1M in this data and none reached $10M. The base rate is brutal.
The women's growth line has not slowed for six years, which is exactly when trends do slow. At saturation the segment lands nearer 22% than 28.3%.
Celsius and Alani Nu share an owner and 24% of multi-outlet. A third brand needs a reason to exist beyond 'not them'.
Convenience is the slowest-growing major channel and it is the only one this SKU data can see.

price_correction.was: $0.25-0.30/oz holds 33.9% of single-serve revenue at $7.4M per SKU, double any other band.
price_correction.why: The per-ounce framing was read off the whole category, where the high-yield band is 79.5% 12 oz cans. Conditioning on the 16 oz format this brand actually sells inverts the instruction — the same dataset that appears to recommend a premium per-ounce position recommends the opposite once size is held constant.

ecom.caveat: Scraped on four search terms only (Celsius, Alani Nu, Ghost, Monster), so it cannot measure brand share — Red Bull appears with six listings purely because nobody searched for it. What it can show is which kinds of brand and which claims exist on Amazon at all, and that is the part used here.

scaled.note: Cell dollars are the convenience-measured flavor mix lifted to all-channel scale using each audience's Euromonitor Passport share — flavor proportions come from PDI because nothing else sees flavor, while the scale comes from Passport because convenience alone understates audiences selling online or through grocery.
scaled.caveat: Three audiences are shown at convenience scale only: Passport lists no brands for them, so their all-channel figure would be zero. That is a gap in Passport's coverage rather than an absence of sales, and rescaling by it would have erased the only measurements available. Their cells are therefore not comparable in dollars with the rescaled rows.

price_grid.note: Singles only — a multipack price divided by a single-can size invents a premium tier that is not there. Band membership is average realised price over each SKU's life, so these are positioning tiers rather than shelf tags.
price_grid.headline: Pooled across formats the top-yielding rung looks like $3.00–3.49. That is 12 oz economics leaking through: at 12 oz it earns $6.93M per SKU. Hold size at the 16 oz can this brand actually sells and the answer inverts — $2.50–2.99 returns $3.09M per SKU against $2.02M one rung up. Same dataset, opposite instruction.

data_quality.note: The extract groups by barcode AND canonical brand, and PDI reassigns a barcode when a product changes brand — AMP becoming Mtn Dew Energy, for instance. Those are genuinely two commercial periods for one physical can, so the rows are not junk, but they are not distinct products either. Revenue is unaffected: the rows partition it rather than duplicating it, and both files still total $7.124B exactly.
data_quality.impact: The count of distinct products on this site was previously given as 2,309. That is the row count; the number of distinct barcodes is 2,178. Every revenue figure, share and ranking is unchanged — only the product count was overstated, by 6%. The 131 affected barcodes carry 1.36% of revenue and none of them disagree about flavor.
